assessment.mechanisms: All 30 accepted findings across three rounds are one mechanism: the guard reads a command's text statically and each report found a place where that reading disagreed with what gh (pflag precedence, attached values, string slices, aliases), curl (option clusters, globs, userinfo, ports, fragments), bash and PowerShell (environment inheritance), or GitHub (REST path canonicalization, GraphQL traversals from any entry point, boolean search semantics) actually do. Every one is in the switch-on position only; the off position, which is what merges and runs until #1967, was compared against origin/main by three reviewers (1152, 22 and 832 sampled decisions) with no difference, and the corrections are reached only under repos.cutover or are explicitly split on it. From round 2 the corrections stopped modelling the tools and replaced each class with a fail-closed rule (any mention of the code repository refuses; every whole API URL is a destination; unknown GraphQL entry points refuse), and the round 3 undirected correction at 3626459970 goes furthest: a curl argument naming GitHub with a glob character is refused outright, any GraphQL selection of issues, comments, reviews, discussions or timelines is refused whatever repository it names, a search with OR is unscoped, and every curl destination is checked for internal typed creation. These prevent the class rather than patch instances, at the cost of disclosed over-refusals.
assessment.regressions: Corrections introduced at least three defects in earlier rounds, all found by the next reviewer: round 1's 'value of the preceding flag' exclusion produced the -XGET destination leak; round 1's 'a quoted word with a space is not a flag' rule hid --body=<url> selectors; round 3's -g detection and range-first-value glob expansion produced round 3 undirected findings 1 and 6. Each regression came from modelling a tool's syntax; the final commit removes those models. That history is exactly why the final correction, which again changes switch-on behaviour and has had no independent review, should be read once more rather than accepted on the writer's verification alone. Stability of the off position has never been in question.
assessment.repairOptions: The broader alternative is allow-lists: only enumerated gh subcommands and REST paths on the code repository and no GraphQL at all. It would close the long tail of exotic forms but risks refusing commands #1963 to #1965 need at cutover, and the ticket scopes the hook as a guardrail against forgetting the type or the repository, not against evasion. The writer's fail-closed rules already cover every form an agent retargeting a command by mistake would produce; most of round 3's findings (cross-owner GraphQL traversal, host globs, attached-value tricks, OR searches) are evasion-grade. I agree with keeping the current rules and not moving to allow-lists. One simplification is worth the round 4 reviewer's attention: the new glob refusal exempts arguments holding a quote or a space as bodies, while HTTP_URL also excludes quotes, so a GitHub URL glob argument that carries a quoted query string may be neither refused as a glob nor read as a destination; if curl sends it and GitHub answers, the simpler rule is to drop the body exemption for any argument that starts with a GitHub URL.
assessment.residualRisk: 1. Switch off, which merges and runs until #1967: none found by any reviewer; decisions match origin/main and the committed repos.json was never flipped. 2. Switch on: the final correction at 3626459970 is unreviewed and behaviour-changing; given three correction-introduced defects earlier, a further leak or over-refusal in its four blanket rules is plausible (the quoted-query glob gap above is one candidate). Beyond that, forms outside the static scope the PR discloses (variables, earlier exports, query files, curl -K, other clients, aliases, wrappers) remain by design. 3. Over-refusals accepted on the fail-closed side are listed in the PR's Notes; the one most likely to bite at cutover is that GraphQL ticket reads on the internal repository are refused, so #1963 to #1965 must use gh issue -R or REST, and no current skill text uses gh api graphql.

unrelated request fields falsely establish REST search scope

assessment.mechanisms: Of the 14 accepted findings across three rounds, 9 come from one mechanism: the hand-written Markdown reader that decides which `#N` the rewrite may map, which split text into code and prose before it knew the block structure (round 1 data #1 link destinations; round 1 undirected #1 fence boundaries; round 2 #1 list marker closing a fence and #2 balanced parentheses in a destination; round 3 #1 to #4 false block boundaries, a backtick in a link title, an unclosed list fence, mid-line definitions), and the writer's own corpus measurement found two more classes of the same mechanism (a code span ends with its block; GitHub links `#N` after `/`, `-` and an en dash). The other five are independent and each closed as a class: a closed reason applied only on a state change; verify omitting title, author and creation time and not comparing computed closing references both ways; restore skipping absent values and archived items; a lost rehearsal creation outside cleanup's reach; a partial journal line swallowing the next record. The round 3 correction at aa378fd55 restructures the reader (about 330 lines) in CommonMark's order rather than patching it a fifth time: fenced blocks by blockquote depth and list container first, then per-block spans, code elements and links left to right, definitions only at a block start. Its evidence is strong but author-provided: 41 tests with the new rows red at 720b408e3, all 46 test inputs rendered through GitHub's Markdown API, agreement with marked on all 2,441 live texts, agreement with GitHub's renderer on 476 of 480 rendered texts, and rehearsal 4 passing verify end to end. The mechanism that remains is not in the reader but in verify: it derives each expected text with the same reader as the rewrite, so a misreading on a form outside the measured corpus (a ticket filed before the cutover, for instance) would leave a bare old number pointing at the wrong internal ticket and verify would still pass. Round 3's reviewer proved this with six misread bodies that runVerify accepted; the writer and both later adjudications name it as the outstanding gap.
assessment.regressions: One correction introduced a defect: round 2's block-boundary rule (a `|` line or any ordered marker ends a span) produced round 3 finding 1, and its table fixture was itself wrong. The round 3 restructuring replaces that rule with real block boundaries, but it is a large unreviewed change of the same kind that regressed once before, so it needs an independent round before anything is accepted. No other correction was reported as introducing a defect, and the five independent fixes held through later rounds.
assessment.repairOptions: A broader repair exists and is the right next step: make verify independent of the reader. Render each migrated text's original through GitHub's Markdown API in the public repository's context and its final text in the internal repository's context, and check that every reference GitHub links in the final text is the map's image of the corresponding reference GitHub links in the original, in order, with the exact-text comparison kept as it is. That turns verify from a restatement of the rewrite's own reading into an oracle that cannot share its mistakes, at about two renders per text with a reference (about 3,400 requests, inside the hourly budget). The stronger alternative, taking the reference positions from GitHub at snapshot time with sentinel numbers so the rewrite needs no reader at all, is larger, changes the snapshot and the rewrite together, and is not needed once verify is independent: a misreading then fails the migration's verify instead of silently landing. The render-based verify is what the checkpoint guidance calls for when a mechanism's failure mode is false assurance, and it keeps the Feature's agreed behaviour (the verify mode still reports zero bare old references and exits non-zero on any difference). It is new behaviour and must be reviewed together with the reader rewrite in one bounded round once built and verified.

checkpoints.limitReason: The unreviewed range is one commit that adds the rewrite gate and its fallback and fixes the oracle; one bounded round with a single undirected reviewer covers it, and the gate bounds what any further reader finding can do, so a sweep of more Markdown forms is no longer the question.

assessment.mechanisms: Round 4 added seven accepted findings: six more Markdown forms the hand-written reader misreads (a blank line inside <pre>, a fence in nested list items, a table with mismatched delimiter cells, a multi-line definition, a setext heading or thematic break, a quoted title right after an angle-bracket destination), which brings the reader's share to 15 of 21 accepted findings, and one hole in the render oracle itself: a stand-in per token broke a reference link whose label held the number, and the oracle then endorsed the broken link. The reviewer also noted that four of the six misreads changed protected text in ways neither the exact-text comparison nor the render check could see, because the render check only compares issue links. The correction at 51a6a7c0c stops relying on the reader being right: before rewriting a text, the tool renders its original twice in the code repository's context, once with a stand-in per token (which tokens GitHub links) and once with a stand-in per number (which numbers it links, in order, with every label and definition kept equal), and rewrites only when its reading maps exactly those tokens and numbers; a text where they disagree is left as the transfer wrote it, where GitHub itself qualified every reference outside code spans, with only the body's migration line restored, listed under leftAsTransferred and journaled so reruns and verify read the answer. Verify's render check moves to a stand-in per number, closing the oracle hole, and the reader now protects an inline link's text, which GitHub never links. I read the diff: the gate compares reader tokens against GitHub-linked tokens and reader numbers against GitHub-linked numbers in order, a misreading that moves, adds or drops a reference therefore refuses the text, and the journaled result is consulted by both rewrite and verify. Against GitHub's real renderer the gate refuses all seven round 4 inputs and accepts four controls; on the 480-text live sample it refuses none once link text is protected; rehearsal 7 passed with nothing left as transferred.
assessment.regressions: None found in round 4 for the round 3 and repair commits beyond the oracle hole, which is a gap in the new render check rather than a regression of earlier behaviour: the per-token stand-in could change a reference link's identity, so digits-only substitution was not meaning-preserving in that one construct. The gate's per-number render repairs it, and the render check now uses the same. The gate itself is new behaviour no reviewer has seen, and it changes the rewrite, which previous rounds had reviewed as unconditional; that is the reason not to accept 51a6a7c0c unreviewed.
assessment.repairOptions: The gate is the broad repair: instead of a sixth patch to the reader, it bounds what any misreading can do to a refusal that keeps GitHub's own qualified text. The remaining alternative, taking reference positions from GitHub alone and dropping the reader, would give the same safety at a higher refusal rate and a larger rewrite of the tool; it is not needed while the gate refuses none of the measured corpus. One point for the round 5 reviewer rather than a change now: a refused text keeps bare old numbers inside code spans (GitHub's transfer rewrite qualifies references in fences and prose but leaves code spans alone), so the Feature's grep criterion for bare old numbers should treat code spans the way the tool does, and the final report must list every text left as transferred so the maintainer can read them.
assessment.residualRisk: 1. The gate and the fallback are unreviewed: a misreading now slips through only if the reader's tokens and numbers both match GitHub's two renders by coincidence, or where GitHub links nothing on either side (a number changed inside code when the reader and GitHub agree on every linked token), which the exact-text comparison still covers against the tool's own target for rewritten texts. 2. A text left as transferred keeps GitHub's qualified references, so its migrated references read ImpowerGames/impower#old and resolve by redirect rather than carrying the new internal number; this is a bounded, reported deviation from the Feature's rewrite rule that affected zero of the 480 sampled live texts, and the maintainer is told of it in the coordinator's report. 3. The window now needs about 7,400 renders (3,700 for the gate, 3,700 for verify), about 1.7 hours of the request budget, on top of the write hours already disclosed. 4. Operational limits unchanged: 120-second settle tested on three-issue runs, 7.5 plus 3.8 hours of writes, no REST re-archive, duplicates' canonical links, sub-issue order; rehearsals and other activity have consumed internal numbers through 30, so the migration starts at 31 or later. 5. CI on 51a6a7c0c is green after two reruns of the Windows driver tier for process-fixture flakes in untouched tests (clean-worktrees and the test-suite runner's own test, the #1810 and #1999 classes).
assessment.coverage: At 51a6a7c0c: node --test scripts/migrate-tracker.test.mjs passes 47 cases; three of the new or changed tests fail against 6f5769ab5's tool in a scratch tree (the gate refusing a misread body, link text staying unmapped, per-number stand-ins), the fourth passing there for a stated reason; the gate refuses all seven round 4 inputs and accepts four controls through GitHub's real renderer; the gate refuses none of the 480-text live sample after link text is protected; marked agrees with the reader on all 2,441 texts with link text excluded the same way; rehearsal 7 (public #2041-#2043 to internal #28-#30) ran 6 gate renders, left nothing as transferred, rewrote 3 bodies and 1 comment, compared 6 links with 0 differences, passed verify and deleted everything from both repositories; every CI check passed on the head. Not covered: an independent reviewer's reading of the gate and the fallback, and the reviewer's own local runs in round 4, which the shared test reservation refused.
assessment.nextRoundValue: One bounded round with a single undirected reviewer over 6f5769ab5..51a6a7c0c establishes whether the gate's two-render agreement is sound (a reader misreading cannot pass both renders except by the coincidence named above), whether leaving a text as transferred is always safe (what such a text holds inside code spans and on its migration line, and how verify and the final report treat it), whether the journaled gate resumes correctly, and whether the per-number render check still locates each reference. That is the review the new behaviour needs before anything is accepted.
assessment.rationale: Round 4 found seven more findings, so the defect class has not stopped recurring in the reader, and the correction is new behaviour that changes the rewrite and that no reviewer has read; accepting it unreviewed fails both conditions for an acceptance. The merge gate admits only the last reviewed head (6f5769ab5, with seven accepted unfixed findings) or an accepted head. The correction is the kind of repair the guidance asks for when one mechanism keeps producing findings (it removes the reader's power to write a wrong text rather than patching its instances), and the guidance then calls for a bounded round on it. So the decision is a one-round extension, limit 5, with one undirected reviewer recommended over the gate commit, and the next checkpoint after round 5's verified fixes. The Feature's agreed behaviour is read as preserved: every text the tool rewrites still follows the rewrite rule, the acceptance criteria are unchanged, and the fallback is a reported safety net that affected no sampled text; the coordinator reports the fallback's semantics to the maintainer, who can object.
